analysis.one_liner: Requires warning labels on sugary and ultra-processed foods and bans junk-food advertising aimed at children.
analysis.headline: Introduced with bipartisan sponsorship from one Republican, the bill has had no committee hearing or vote since its November 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require prominent health warnings on the front of sugary drinks, diet products with non-sugar sweeteners, ultra-processed foods, and foods high in sugar, saturated fat, or sodium — with the first two carrying an explicit "not recommended for children" statement. It would make it unlawful to market those products to children under 13, restore the Federal Trade Commission's authority to regulate children's advertising (limited by Congress in 1980), and fund federal nutrition research and a public education campaign. It was introduced on November 25, 2025, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has remained with no action.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and their families gain the most: parents would see plain warnings — including "not recommended for children" — on sugary drinks and diet products, junk-food ads aimed at kids under 13 would become unlawful, and new federally funded research and public education would target diet-related disease. Shoppers generally gain clearer front-of-package information, including on vending machines and online listings. Over time, the intended payoff is lower rates of childhood obesity and type 2 diabetes.

how_it_helps.text: Requires bold, bordered FDA warnings on the front of packages — covering 5% of the front, plus vending machines, multi-packs, and online listings — for sugar-sweetened beverages, foods with non-sugar sweeteners, ultra-processed foods, and foods high in added sugar, saturated fat, or sodium. Sugary drinks and artificially sweetened products must say they are "not recommended for children."

Makes it unlawful to market or advertise any of those products to children under 13 using cartoons, influencers, celebrity endorsements, toys, or ads in media where children are 30% or more of the audience, and requires the warning labels to appear in any ads for these products. It repeals the 1980 provision that stripped the FTC's power to write rules on children's advertising.

Authorizes $60 million a year for NIH research on how ultra-processed foods affect health, $10 million a year for a CDC public education campaign on nutrition and the new labels, and $5 million a year for the FDA to write and enforce the labeling rules, for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

Directs the National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine to convene experts and recommend a scientific definition of "ultra-processed food" for the FDA to use, and requires majority of participants in federal nutrition meetings to have no financial ties to ultra-processed food manufacturers.

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage manufacturers bear the direct costs: redesigned labels and packaging covering 5% of the front of the package, warning displays on vending machines and online listings, lost child-directed marketing, and potential FTC penalties. Advertising agencies, media companies, and digital platforms lose junk-food ad revenue aimed at children. Compliance costs would likely be passed on to consumers in prices, and taxpayers fund the authorized appropriations — up to $75 million per year for fiscal years 2026-2030 if Congress actually appropriates the money.

drawbacks.text: The label mandates are expensive and broad: warnings must take up at least 5% of the front of every covered package and appear on multi-packs, vending machines, and online listings, and packaging redesign costs would ultimately be passed on to shoppers.

The interim definition of "ultra-processed food" sweeps in products containing common industrial ingredients such as emulsifiers, flavoring agents, and stabilizers, so many ordinary grocery staples could carry a warning linking them to weight gain and diabetes until the National Academies delivers a tighter definition a year or more after enactment.

Diet drinks and products sweetened with stevia, aspartame, or sucralose would carry a "not recommended for children" warning even though many parents use them specifically to cut sugar, and the ban on child-directed advertising plus the restored FTC rulemaking power would almost certainly draw First Amendment lawsuits and years of industry litigation.
The bill authorizes but does not guarantee funding: the $75 million per year for research, education, and enforcement depends on separate annual appropriations votes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside is real: front-of-package warning labels have been shown in other countries to change what people buy, and a ban on marketing junk food to children under 13 directly targets how those habits form. The main costs fall on the food, beverage, and advertising industries, not on government budgets — though some of it reaches consumers through prices. The bill's weak points are its sweeping interim definition of ultra-processed food, which risks mislabeling everyday staples, and its likelihood of protracted court challenges over the advertising ban. An honest supporter would concede the bill as written could use a tighter definition and a longer runway; an honest opponent would concede the current labeling system gives parents almost nothing at the moment of choice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Representative Don Beyer introduced the bill on November 25, 2025, joined by Representatives Scott Peters and Mike Lawler, making the original sponsorship bipartisan with one Republican.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which handles food and drug law.
No further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no vote — has been recorded since the referral, and the bill sits in committee while Congress remains in session until January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, food and beverage makers and their advertisers: the bill imposes nothing on them while it sits in committee, and with only three cosponsors and no committee movement, the labels and the children's advertising ban it would create are not happening.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Food and beverage marketers, so far

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, so the partisan shape is unknown; early support is 2 of 217 House Democrats plus 1 of 223 House Republicans.

industries.industry: Soda, snack, and ultra-processed food makers
industries.note: The bill puts bold health warnings on the front of their packages — including "not recommended for children" on sugary and artificially sweetened drinks — and outlaws marketing their products to children under 13 using cartoons, influencers, toys, and celebrity tie-ins. Their core sales strategy of colorful packaging and kid-focused advertising is directly targeted, and compliance costs would be substantial.

Child-directed junk-food advertising becomes unlawful, and any ad for covered products must carry the warning label, cutting revenue from children's programming, social media influencer content, and apps where children are 30% or more of the audience. The bill also restores the FTC's 1980-era power to write binding rules on children's advertising, which the industry helped get curtailed.

Products containing aspartame, sucralose, stevia, monk fruit, and similar sweeteners would need a warning saying they are not recommended for children, dampening demand for a category often marketed as a healthy alternative to sugar.

Retailers must display the warnings on vending and self-service machines and carry them on online listings, adding compliance work, but they sell whatever manufacturers produce and face no direct ban on their sales.

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces long odds. Most bills referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee never reach a vote, and this one has drawn only three cosponsors and no committee action since introduction. A committee hearing on ultra-processed food is plausible given current attention to the topic, but the labeling mandates and the children's advertising ban would need an active chair and leadership support to advance, and a standalone floor vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027 is unlikely unless the bill picks up substantial cosponsors or rides along with a larger food or health package.
